Start

Before you begin

What you build · the files · the tools · the time budget

Mercadillo 505, a fictional online market in Madrid, keeps its orders in one flat CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file of 1,955 order lines. In this lab you find out what is wrong with the file, design a relational database for it, build that database in PostgreSQL, load the data, and show that the database refuses the errors that the file accepted. It is the path of Lesson 2 of Class 1: from data that nobody checks to data protected by a DBMS (Database Management System).

The files of the lab

The four files are stored inside this page. Save them into one folder, for example IT505/lab1.

The tools and techniques proposed in this lab are open. You may replace any of them by another tool that is suitable and available to you — SQLite, MariaDB, the psql command line, a notebook — as long as you say which one you used and why. Be creative: research your tools thoroughly, compare at least two before you choose, and write a small tool of your own (a script, a query, a macro) wherever that helps.

Step 0

Choose your data and write five business questions

Class 1 · Monday 23 November 2026 · 20 minutes in the studio + 10 minutes at home
Why this step. A database is built to answer questions. Questions written before the design tell you which data the tables must hold.

Put mercadillo505_orders_flat.csv into your lab folder and open it in a plain-text editor — never in a spreadsheet program, which changes dates and numbers when it saves the file. Read line 1: it names the 13 columns. Then read three or four lines of data.

Write five questions that the manager of the market would ask, in business words and without any SQL (Structured Query Language). At least two questions must involve more than one kind of thing, for example customers and products.

A useful question names what is counted or added up, for which group, and over which period: “Which five products bring in the most money?”
✔ Done when: five numbered questions are saved in your lab folder.
Step 1

Profile the flat file and load it

Class 2 · Tuesday 24 November 2026 · 35 minutes in the studio + 10 minutes at home
Why this step. You cannot design tables for data that you have not inspected. The problem list that you write here becomes the list of rules that your database enforces in Step 3.

In the text editor, note three things about the file: the delimiter (the character between two values), the quote character (the character that encloses a value which itself contains the delimiter) and the text encoding (UTF-8, Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit).

Open a DuckDB connection. In DBeaver: Database → New Database Connection → DuckDB, choose a path such as IT505/lab1/mercadillo.duckdb, press Finish and accept the download of the driver.[1] Without installation rights, use DuckDB in the browser. Then read the file in the simplest way and count the columns of the result. If DuckDB does not find the file, write its full path between the quotes.

SQL
SELECT * FROM 'mercadillo505_orders_flat.csv' LIMIT 5;
What it means. A flat file declares no structure. Every program that reads it has to guess the delimiter and the types, and one malformed line is enough to make the guess fail. A database stores the structure together with the data.

Tell the reader to set malformed lines apart, and ask which lines they were. Then find that line in the text editor and write down what is wrong with it.

SQL
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM read_csv('mercadillo505_orders_flat.csv', store_rejects = true);
SELECT line, error_type, error_message FROM reject_errors;
You should see 1,954 readable rows and one rejected line: line 919, TOO MANY COLUMNS, “Expected Number of Columns: 13 Found: 14”.

Load the readable rows into a table, every value as text, then look at the profile of the file. SUMMARIZE shows, for every column, the type that DuckDB guessed, an estimate of the number of distinct values and the percentage of empty cells. Why did order_date not become a date?

SQL
CREATE TABLE orders_flat AS
  SELECT * FROM read_csv('mercadillo505_orders_flat.csv', ignore_errors = true, all_varchar = true);
SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM read_csv('mercadillo505_orders_flat.csv', ignore_errors = true);

Write the problem list: at least five kinds of problem. For each kind give the query that shows it, one example, the number of rows and the term of Lesson 2 that names it. Two queries to start from are below; for the other kinds, look at the dates, at the empty cells, and at the e-mail addresses next to the names.

SQL
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders_flat GROUP BY city ORDER BY city;
SELECT order_id, product, COUNT(*) AS copies FROM orders_flat GROUP BY ALL HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Your problem list has this shape. The first line is filled in as an example:

#Kind of problemQuery that shows itOne exampleRowsTerm of Lesson 2
1One malformed linereject_errorsline 919: a comma inside a value without quotes1no enforced rule
2……………
3……………
4……………
5……………

Answer those of your five questions that one table can answer, and save the queries as lab1_step1.sql. Note which questions the flat table answers badly, and why. An example of the form, for the question “Which five products bring in the most money?”:

SQL
SELECT product, SUM(CAST(unit_price AS DECIMAL(8,2)) * CAST(quantity AS INTEGER)) AS revenue
FROM orders_flat GROUP BY product ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 5;
You should see five products; the first one is Esparto basket with 1776.00 €. Because of the duplicated lines, this total is too high: a reason to build the database.
✔ Done when: you have the problem list and lab1_step1.sql.
Step 2

Business rules, diagram, schema

Class 3 · Wednesday 25 November 2026 · 30 minutes in the studio + 10 minutes at home
Why this step. The design is decided on paper, where a change costs nothing. Rules written as sentences can be checked by somebody who knows the business and no SQL.

Write at least six business rules as sentences. A rule says how many of one thing can belong to another thing: “A customer places zero or more orders.” “An order belongs to exactly one customer.” “An order line is one product in one order, with a quantity.”

Draw the ERD (Entity-Relationship Diagram): the entities, the identifier of each one, and every relationship with its “how many” at both ends. Use drawDB in the browser[4], or paper and a phone camera. One order holds several products, and one product appears in many orders: which entity links them, and where does the quantity live?

Fill in a schema sheet: one block per table, with its columns, their types, the primary key and the foreign keys. Bring the schema to 3NF (third normal form): every column that is not part of the key depends on the key, on the whole key, and on nothing but the key. One block looks like this:

Schema sheet
Table categories — one row per product category
  category_id   INTEGER   primary key, generated by the database
  name          TEXT      NOT NULL, UNIQUE
✔ Done when: the schema has at least four tables and stores no fact twice — the city of a customer once, the category of a product once.
Step 3

Build, load and test in PostgreSQL

Class 4 · Thursday 26 November 2026 · 35 minutes in the studio + 10 minutes at home
Why this step. A rule that exists only in a document protects nothing. Declared in the database, the same rule is enforced on every row, for every user.

Create a database called mercadillo and write schema.sql: one CREATE TABLE statement per table, parents before children, with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES, NOT NULL and at least two CHECK rules. The two tables below are an example of the form; your tables come from your schema sheet.

SQL
CREATE DATABASE mercadillo;

-- parent first
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

-- then the child, which refers to the parent
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date  DATE NOT NULL,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (customer_id)
);

Create a staging table that takes the file as it is, every column as text, and import the file into it: in DBeaver, right-click the table and choose Import Data[1]; in psql, use \copy. What happens at the malformed line depends on the tool: the COPY command of PostgreSQL refuses the whole file, and an import wizard may load the line with its values moved one column to the right. In both cases, repair the line in a copy of the file — put the product name between double quotes — import again, and say in the report what you changed.

SQL
CREATE TABLE staging_orders (order_id TEXT, order_date TEXT, customer_name TEXT,
  customer_email TEXT, city TEXT, referred_by TEXT, product TEXT, category TEXT,
  producer TEXT, unit_price TEXT, quantity TEXT, payment_method TEXT, status TEXT);

-- psql: import the repaired copy of the file (use your own path)
\copy staging_orders FROM 'mercadillo505_orders_flat_repaired.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)
You should see COPY 1955: 1,955 rows in the staging table.

Write load.sql: fill the clean tables from the staging table, parents first, with INSERT INTO … SELECT DISTINCT …. The two patterns are below. Decide, and justify in one sentence each: which column identifies a customer whose name is typed in several ways; how the two date formats become one DATE; which spelling of each city is kept; what happens to a line that has no quantity.

SQL
-- a parent table: one row per distinct value
INSERT INTO categories (name)
SELECT DISTINCT category FROM staging_orders ORDER BY category;

-- a child table: the key of the parent is looked up with a join
INSERT INTO products (name, category_id, unit_price)
SELECT DISTINCT s.product, c.category_id, s.unit_price::numeric(8,2)
FROM staging_orders s JOIN categories c ON c.name = s.category;

Useful functions: TRIM(x) removes the spaces at both ends; NULLIF(x, '') turns an empty text into NULL; to_date(x, 'DD/MM/YYYY') reads a day/month/year text as a date; CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END chooses between two conversions.

Never convert a day/month/year text with ::date. The database accepts some of these dates and reads them wrongly:
StatementResult in PostgreSQLReading
SELECT '05/11/2026'::date;2026-05-11accepted, and wrong: read as 11 May
SELECT '21/11/2026'::date;ERROR: date/time field value out of range: "21/11/2026"refused, because there is no month 21
SELECT to_date('05/11/2026', 'DD/MM/YYYY');2026-11-05correct: 5 November

Compare your row counts with the file. A different number is not automatically wrong: explain it with one of your loading decisions.

What you countReference value
orders718
products35
customers154
distinct order lines in the file1,937

Write three integrity tests: three INSERT statements that the database must refuse — a duplicated key, a reference to a row that does not exist, and a value that breaks a CHECK or NOT NULL rule. Copy each statement and its error message into the report.

SQL
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, order_date, customer_id, status)
VALUES ('M505-1047', '2026-11-22', 1, 'shipped');
-- ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey"
✔ Done when: schema.sql and load.sql run without error from an empty database, and the three tests are refused.
Report

Write the report and hand in

By Sunday 6 December 2026, 23:59 · 20 minutes at home

The report has five pages at most and is handed in as a PDF (Portable Document Format) file. Introduction: the data and your five questions. Body: the problem list, the business rules, the diagram, the schema, your loading decisions, the row counts and the three tests. Conclusion: what the database guarantees that the file did not, and which of your questions wait for Lab 2. Cite your sources in APA (American Psychological Association) style, and end with a paragraph “Tools and sources” that names every tool you used, with its version and its licence.

Hand-in check-list

IT505_Lab1_Surname.pdf — the report, five pages at most

schema.sql — runs from an empty database

load.sql — fills the tables, parents first

The diagram as an image

Rules

  • Honest work. You may read documentation and forums, and you may use an automated assistant to understand a concept or an error message. The design, the SQL (Structured Query Language) and the text that you hand in must be your own, and you must be able to explain every line of them. Name every aid that you used under “Tools and sources”. The University's Academic Honesty Policy applies in full.
  • Fictional or open data only. Never load personal information about real people; in the European Union such data are protected by the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation).
  • Official downloads only. Before you install a tool, find its licence on the list of the Open Source Initiative.
Help

If something goes wrong

Six frequent situations, with their cause and remedy
What you seeCause and remedy
DuckDB: No files found that match the patternThe path is wrong. Write the full path of the file between single quotes, with forward slashes.
DBeaver asks to download a driverAccept. The first connection to each kind of database downloads its driver and needs the internet.
PostgreSQL: relation "customers" does not existA child table is created before its parent. Change the order of the statements.
PostgreSQL: date/time field value out of rangeThe file holds two date formats. Keep the dates as text in the staging table and convert them in load.sql.
The tables are empty after the loadDBeaver is in manual-commit mode. Press Commit, or switch to Auto-commit.
Odd dates or numbers in the fileThe file was saved by a spreadsheet program. Download the starter file again from this page.

Still blocked? Bring the exact message to the next studio block: the studios of Classes 1 to 4 each hold a block for this lab.

Version notes

The animations are schematic screens drawn for this guide. Every result and every message in them is the real output of the tool named in its title bar.

  1. Menu names as in DBeaver Community 26.2.5 (15 November 2026), the current release on 20 November 2026. A newer release may name or place a menu differently; the steps stay the same.
  2. Results captured on 20 November 2026 with DuckDB 2.0.1 and repeated with 2.0.0. On that day duckdb.org listed 2.0.0, and the Python package 2.0.1 was published. Another version may guess the structure of the file differently in action 4; actions 5 to 8 do not depend on that guess.
  3. Messages captured on 20 November 2026 with PostgreSQL 16.15. The statements are standard SQL and exist unchanged in PostgreSQL 18.7 (recommended for the course this week) and 19.0 (released on 19 November 2026); the wording of a message may differ slightly in another version.
  4. drawDB was opened and checked on 20 November 2026: the editor is open source and needs no account. Its extra services (storage in the cloud, an assistant) need a sign-in and are not needed for this lab.
